tagline: Plain-English fund reviews. Low costs win.
_tokens_note: Analytics, verification, contact-form and affiliate values are no longer stored here — they live in config.json / config.local.json and are injected by build.py.

author.name: Nathan Blake
author.title: Editor, Mutual Fund Reviewer
author.bio: Nathan Blake has spent fifteen years writing about index investing, retirement accounts, and the quiet math of expense ratios. He is not a licensed financial advisor, and nothing on this site is personalized investment advice — he is an editor who reads prospectuses so you don't have to. His own portfolio is three index funds and a rebalancing calendar reminder.

robos.name: Betterment
robos.best_for: Hands-off investors who want automatic rebalancing and tax-loss harvesting without thinking about it
robos.summary: Betterment is the largest independent robo-advisor and the most polished version of the hands-off pitch: deposit money, answer a few questions, and it builds a diversified ETF portfolio it rebalances automatically. The 0.25% fee is roughly six times what you'd pay holding a total-market index fund yourself — that's the honest trade. What you get for it is behavioral guardrails, automated tax-loss harvesting in taxable accounts, and goal-based buckets that make it harder to tinker.
robos.verdict: Worth it if automation keeps you invested. Not worth it if you're already comfortable buying VTSAX or FZROX on a schedule.
pros: Tax-loss harvesting on taxable accounts at no extra cost
Clean goal-based interface that discourages tinkering
cons: 0.25% fee is ~6x a DIY three-fund portfolio
You don't pick the underlying funds
Premium tier (human advice) requires a large balance

robos.name: Wealthfront
robos.best_for: Investors who want robo automation plus a high-yield cash account in one place
robos.summary: Wealthfront runs the same basic playbook as Betterment — diversified ETF portfolios, automatic rebalancing, tax-loss harvesting — with a stronger software bent. Its direct indexing (buying individual S&P 500 stocks to harvest more losses) kicks in at higher balances and is a real, if modest, tax edge. The cash account consistently pays competitive yields, which makes it a reasonable single home for emergency fund plus long-term money.
robos.verdict: The strongest pure-software robo. Same caveat as all of them: the 0.25% only earns its keep if the automation changes your behavior.
pros: Direct indexing at higher balances improves tax-loss harvesting
cons: No human advisors at any tier
0.25% fee on money you could index yourself for ~0.04%

robos.name: M1 Finance
robos.best_for: DIY investors who want automation around their own fund picks rather than someone else's portfolio
robos.summary: M1 sits between a brokerage and a robo. You build a 'pie' of funds or stocks — say 60% VTI, 30% VXUS, 10% BND — and M1 automates the rest: every deposit buys whatever slice is underweight. It's the closest thing to a self-directed robo, and for index investors who already know what they want to hold, it removes the last excuse for not rebalancing.
robos.verdict: The best fit for readers of this site: you keep control of the funds, M1 handles the discipline.
pros: You choose the exact ETFs; M1 automates contributions and rebalancing
Fee is flat and waived above $10,000
Fractional shares make small contributions efficient
cons: No mutual funds — ETFs and stocks only
Limited trading windows (one or two per day)

robos.name: Interactive Brokers
robos.fee: $0 commissions on US stocks/ETFs (IBKR Lite); mutual fund fees vary
robos.best_for: Cost-obsessed investors and anyone who wants access to nearly every fund and market on earth
robos.summary: Interactive Brokers is a full brokerage, not a robo, and it earns its place here for one reason: it is relentlessly cheap. IBKR Lite offers commission-free US stock and ETF trades, the margin rates are the lowest in the industry by a wide margin, and the mutual fund marketplace includes thousands of no-transaction-fee funds. The interface assumes you know what you're doing.
robos.verdict: The power-user choice. If 'minimize every basis point' is your religion, this is your church — just expect a learning curve.
pros: Lowest all-in costs of any major broker
Enormous fund and ETF selection, including international markets
Industry-best margin rates if you ever need them
cons: Interface is built for professionals and feels like it
No automated portfolio management on the basic platform
Customer support is functional, not hand-holding

robos.name: SoFi Invest
robos.fee: 0.25% for automated investing; $0 commissions for self-directed
robos.best_for: Beginners starting with small amounts who want investing, banking, and loans under one roof
robos.summary: SoFi Invest is the friendliest on-ramp on this list. The $1 minimum and fractional shares mean a college student can start a real portfolio with lunch money, and the automated option builds a sensible ETF mix. The catch is depth: the fund lineup is thinner than the big brokerages, and SoFi's own ETFs anchor the automated portfolios.
robos.verdict: A fine place to start; many investors eventually outgrow it. Starting matters more than optimizing, so that's not a knock.
pros: Access to human financial planners at no extra cost
Tight integration with SoFi banking products
cons: Automated portfolios lean on SoFi's own ETFs
Fund research tools are thin compared to Fidelity or Schwab
